Chapter 8. The Detective’s Dilemma.
You know, every mystery has its champions—the folks who just can’t let the past stay buried. Sometimes it’s a journalist, hunched over stacks of old files in a dusty archive. Other times, it’s a family member who can’t shake the questions that haunt them. But the truth is, the hunt for answers isn’t glamorous. It’s more a string of little frustrations: a document that’s nowhere to be found, a phone call that hits a dead end, or a memory that just doesn’t add up.
When it came to Mitchell Siegel’s murder, the detective’s dilemma was simple, but it ran deep. How do you get to the truth when the evidence has disappeared and nobody’s talking? Sure, the official story sounded tidy, but the details? They were a mess. There was a missing police report, a gun that vanished without a trace, and a timeline that never quite clicked. Most people would’ve just moved on, but a handful kept digging, refusing to let the questions go.
Years later, one researcher found herself staring at a faded photograph, wondering what secrets might be hiding in plain sight. She tracked down old neighbors, gathered little scraps of testimony, and tried to piece together a night that history had almost forgotten. It was slow work, and the answers stayed just out of reach. But every now and then, a clue would pop up—a letter, a diary entry, maybe even just something someone let slip—and suddenly, the story would shift.
Most of us don’t realize just how much of history is built on uncertainty. The official version? It’s only one way the story could go, shaped by what people needed or feared at the time. The real story is usually messier, tangled up in contradictions and loose ends. But here’s something to remember: the act of searching—the fact that someone cares enough to keep looking—that’s a kind of justice all its own.
